notes: Personalized RAG demo corpus, rebuilt from scratch around a single, deliberately designed persona: the 'Argument-First Grader'. This instructor cares intensely about the substance of the argument -- precise claims and genuinely integrated reasoning -- and is comparatively indifferent to presentation (formal register, emotional restraint, surface grammar). Strict criteria (W1a-1, W1a-2, WR-1): scored below the rubric anchor for vagueness/hedging or mechanical reasoning, but a genuinely precise/well-reasoned excerpt earns full marks same as the anchor -- the strictness is satisfiable, not a blanket penalty. Lenient criteria (W1d-1, W1d-2, L1-1): scored at/near full marks regardless of informal register, mild loaded language, or grammar slips -- these are deprioritized. Control criteria (W1b-1, W1b-2, W1b-3, W1c-1, W1c-2, W1e-1): no deviation, anchor_matched == score throughout, so live grading shows divergence only on the six deviation criteria.

instructor_profile.grading_philosophy: I care about the strength of the argument itself -- how precise the claim is, how clearly it's set against the strongest opposing view, and how well the reasoning actually connects evidence to the claim. I score those harder than the rubric anchors alone would if a claim is vague or the reasoning is just asserted rather than reasoned through. Presentation is a different matter: I don't take points off for informal register, occasional loaded phrasing, or grammar and spelling slips. If the argument itself is genuinely strong, sloppy delivery doesn't cost anything; if the argument is genuinely weak, polished delivery doesn't rescue it either.

source_essays.text: I think schools should maybe get rid of standardized tests, or at least do less of them, because tests dont really show what a student can do. Some people like tests since they're easy to compare across schools but thats kind of missing the point. Kids just memorize stuff for the test and forget it right after, so it doesnt actually mean they learned anything. A capstone project would probably be better since students would have to actually use what they know. It would take a lot of work to change the whole system though. Basically capstones seem like a better idea overall for actually showing what students can do.

Schools should stop naming a valedictorian, or at least rethink it, because ranking students like that isnt really fair to everyone. Some people think it motivates kids to work harder but that argument doesnt really hold up if you think about it. Ranking one kid above everyone else just makes school feel like a competition instead of learning, and that stresses kids out for no good reason. Getting rid of it would probably make things less stressful for students. There would need to be some other way to recognize achievement I guess. Overall dropping the ranking system just seems like the better move for schools.

I think schools should ban energy drinks on campus, or at least think about limiting them, because kids drink way too much caffeine and it messes with their sleep and focus in class. Some people say its the students own choice what they drink but that kind of ignores that schools already regulate other food and drinks anyway. Kids crash after the caffeine wears off and cant focus for the rest of the day, so it ends up hurting their grades. A ban would probably help with that. It would probably upset some students at first. Overall banning them just makes sense for keeping kids focused during school.

High schools should require a set number of community service hours before graduation, since it connects students to their communities in ways regular classes don't. Critics argue that mandatory service isn't truly service if it's forced, and there's some truth to that concern. However, many students who are required to volunteer report afterward that they wouldn't have sought out the experience on their own, and the exposure itself has value even if the initial motivation was a requirement rather than a personal choice. Community organizations also benefit from a reliable pool of student volunteers, which is a practical advantage worth weighing alongside the philosophical objection. Requiring service hours, then, is a reasonable tradeoff between authenticity and access.

Districts considering a four-day school week should proceed carefully rather than adopting it wholesale, since the research on outcomes is mixed. Proponents point to reduced operating costs and improved teacher retention, both of which are real and measurable benefits. Opponents worry about working parents needing childcare on the fifth day, and that concern deserves a real answer, not a dismissal. A four-day week compresses the same instructional hours into fewer days, which can work well for older students but may not suit younger children's attention spans. Districts should pilot the schedule with willing schools before committing system-wide, so the tradeoffs can be measured rather than assumed.

Requiring a financial literacy course for graduation would give students practical skills that most academic classes don't cover, like budgeting, credit, and taxes. Some argue that this content belongs at home rather than in school, but that assumes every student has a parent equipped to teach it, which isn't a safe assumption to make for an entire district. A required course guarantees a baseline of financial knowledge regardless of a student's home situation. It would mean displacing another elective or requirement, which is a real cost schools would need to weigh. On balance, though, guaranteeing every graduate some financial competency seems worth that tradeoff.

Public high schools should prohibit the sale of single-use plastic bottles and utensils in campus cafeterias, provided that affordable refill and reusable alternatives are made available at the same price point. Opponents rightly note that a ban imposed without infrastructure in place simply shifts inconvenience onto students who cannot afford reusable alternatives, and that objection identifies the actual design requirement rather than a reason to abandon the policy. Where schools have paired plastic bans with subsidized reusable bottles and expanded water-filling stations, waste volumes have dropped substantially without disadvantaging lower-income students, which suggests the objection is a solvable implementation problem rather than a fundamental flaw in the policy itself. The remaining question is one of upfront cost, not of principle: districts must weigh the capital expense of filling stations against the recurring cost of waste disposal and the environmental externality that recurring cost does not capture. On balance, a phased ban paired with guaranteed alternatives addresses the legitimate equity concern while still achieving the environmental goal the policy is meant to serve.

Extending the high school day by thirty minutes, with that time allocated specifically to unstructured academic support rather than additional class instruction, would address a gap that current schedules leave unfilled. Critics argue that students are already fatigued by the end of the day and that additional time would yield diminishing returns, and that concern is legitimate for any proposal that simply adds more direct instruction. Because the proposal here allocates the additional time to flexible, student-directed support rather than another taught period, it responds to fatigue rather than ignoring it, targeting the students who most need extra time without imposing it uniformly on those who don't. Schools that have piloted similar flexible-time blocks report improved completion rates on major assignments, particularly among students balancing coursework with jobs or family responsibilities outside school. The tradeoff is a longer school day for staff as well as students, which is a genuine cost the proposal does not eliminate, only redistributes toward the students most likely to benefit from it.

School dress codes should be rewritten to regulate safety and legibility of identification rather than the specific style, gender presentation, or cultural dress of students, since the current, more expansive codes are enforced unevenly and disproportionately against girls and students of color. Supporters of broader dress codes argue that professional or modest dress prepares students for future workplace expectations, and that goal is a reasonable one for a school to hold. That goal, however, does not require regulating the specific items current codes single out; a narrower code focused on safety and legibility can still require that clothing not obstruct identification or pose a hazard, while removing the provisions that have produced the uneven enforcement. Districts that have already narrowed their codes along these lines report fewer dress-code-related disciplinary referrals overall, with the remaining referrals concentrated on the safety-related provisions the narrower code retains. Rewriting the code to match its actual justification, rather than repealing it outright, preserves the legitimate safety rationale while removing the provisions that were never really about safety at all.
